extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent policy researchers, and policymakers evaluating patent-office resource allocation
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical cost-benefit analysis of investing more examiner time/resources at the Patent Office to reduce issuance of invalid patents and the downstream savings (litigation, PTAB, prosecution, broader social harms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for an invention to be patent eligible, it must be both new and represent a nontrivial advancement over the current state of the art. 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 103 (2012). If an invention was obvious to the person of ordinary skill in the art or was already in the public domain, the invention would have likely arisen without the patent incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory standards reflect a balance between encouraging innovation and avoiding consumer-welfare drains; they are the baseline legal criteria examiners must apply when assessing applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of EPO/JPO outcomes as benchmark for U.S. patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare U.S.-issued patents for which applicants also sought protection at the EPO and the JPO and use outcomes at those foreign offices as a benchmark to assess what the outcome at the U.S. Patent Office would have been if U.S. examiners had more time/resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO and JPO invest substantially more resources per application while having essentially similar patentability standards; this is an imperfect but informative benchmark for marginal-patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner time allocation effect on grant rates
rubrics_metrics.description: A doubling of the amount of time given to examiners is estimated to lower the Patent Office’s grant rate by roughly 27% (or by 19 percentage points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relationship is identified via variation in examiner GS-levels (time allocations vary by GS-level and technology group) and is visualized in regressions of grant incidence on GS-level dummies with 95% confidence intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal patents' legal validity indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents issued as a result of binding time constraints (the marginal patents) are likely to be of questionable legal validity, evidenced by reduced success of those patents at the EPO and JPO relative to patents allowed at lower GS-levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative to patents issued at GS-level 7, patents issued at GS-level 14 are seven percentage points (≈16%) less likely to be allowed by both the EPO and JPO — used as evidence that time-constrained issuances are lower-quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational-ignorance cost-benefit components (Lemley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemley’s analysis limited costs/benefits to: private costs of prosecuting patents, annual returns of licensing patents, and total litigation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemley used these components to argue that doubling examiner hours' costs outweigh benefits; but many empirical relationships were guessed rather than estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions in Lemley’s cost-benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemley assumed (1) doubling examiner time → 10% drop in invalidly issued patents; (2) 10% drop in such patents → 10% drop in litigation costs; (3) doubling examiner time → 50% increase in attorney prosecution costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit numeric assumptions used in his conclusion; the article notes these were guesses due to data limitations and motivates empirical re-estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include broader spectrum of costs of bad patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A fuller accounting should include additional costs Lemley omitted—harms from persistent invalid patents that are never litigated and other social costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (Rai; Ghosh & Kesan) stress that litigation does not perfectly eliminate invalid patents and that unchallenged invalid patents impose nontrivial social costs that should enter cost-benefit calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy decision rule: marginal benefit vs marginal cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether spending one dollar (or a marginal investment) on increasing Patent Office resources would save more than one dollar in downstream costs (litigation, economic harms). If marginal benefits exceed marginal costs, devote more resources to the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article operationalizes this using a doubling-of-hours thought experiment (larger than a $1 marginal change) but discusses scaling to marginal investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three pieces required to estimate litigation savings
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine litigation savings from increased examiner time, researchers need: (1) the costs associated with litigating patents, (2) how many fewer patents would be issued if examiner time increased, and (3) the relationship between examiner review time and the future incidence of litigation for resulting patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemley guessed the latter two; this Article uses empirical methods to estimate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent litigation cost estimates (AIPLA/empirical figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Median cost of patent litigation (AIPLA): when $10–25M at risk, median cost is $1M per side through end of discovery and $2M per side through trial/appeal; when >$25M at risk, $1.7M through discovery and $3M through trial/appeal. PTAB median costs: ~$200K per side through motion practice, $250K through hearing, $350K through appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These empirical cost figures supply the 'costs associated with litigating patents' input for the cost-benefit analysis; numbers scale with amount at risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB as an ex post adjudicatory alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2012 PTAB provides a court-like administrative path for third parties to challenge issued patents; it was intended to be a cost-effective substitute for some federal litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB proceedings mimic trial features (oral arguments, discovery); however, many patents subject to PTAB petitions are also litigated in district courts, and PTAB challenges are not universally substitutive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical method for linking examiner time to litigation outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PAIR data (applications), Lex Machina (federal litigation), PTAB filing data, and an examiner roster (GS-level promotion dates) to merge application-level data with future litigation/PTAB outcomes and examiner GS-level at disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regress the count of times an application/patent is asserted on GS-level dummies using conditional negative binomial models and include fixed effects (technology group) and controls (year disposed, examiner experience bins, examiner join year, examiner ultimate tenure) to isolate time-allocation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of GS-level as proxy for examiner time allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Time allocations are a function of an examiner’s GS-level and the technology group to which the examiner is assigned; GS-level promotions reduce time available per application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification leverages within-technology variation across GS-levels; regressions include technology-group fixed effects to compare within-group GS-level variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline sample choice: filed applications versus issued patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sample of filed applications (not only issued patents) as the baseline so the analysis captures both (1) reductions in issuance volume and (2) reductions in issuance of invalid patents that would spur litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows capturing both theorized mechanisms through which more examiner time reduces overall litigation frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms of invalid patents (catalogue of social costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalid patents can cause supracompetitive pricing (reducing access), preclusion of competitors from markets, stunting of follow-on innovation, opportunistic license-extraction, chilling of venture capital for startups, wasteful litigation costs, and burdens on the judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most of these harms are difficult to quantify precisely; the Article focuses on litigation savings because more empirical data exist for litigation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling considerations for resource increases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Article evaluates a doubling of examiner hours (a large marginal investment) but discusses whether results would generalize to smaller marginal investments; empirical specifications that impose linear time-litigation relationships and nonparametric approaches yield similar savings estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating costs of doubling, conservatively assume overhead, hiring, and staffing costs; scaling concerns addressed empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data inclusion/exclusion and measurement choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical data cover >3.9M utility applications filed on/after March 2001 with final disposition by May 2017 (exclude ongoing applications); estimation sample focuses on applications disposed prior to 2014. Examiner assigned is the individual who did the majority of work (nonsignatory when both present, signatory when only one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These choices ensure complete outcome observation and a consistent assignment of responsibility for examination work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measurement: litigation frequency as count
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure litigation outcomes as the number of times each resulting patent is asserted in litigation (a count variable aggregated by patent number).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lex Machina for federal litigation counts and PTAB filing data for administrative challenges; model counts with negative binomial regressions due to rarity and discrete count nature.
